concepts.decision: Assess cross-boundary trust paths and assign controls/owners at each handoff, not just per tool.
concepts.definition: The interconnected people, identities, tools, repositories, dependencies, environments, pipelines, artifacts, and operational processes used to create and run software.
concepts.failureExample: A secure code repository cannot protect a release if its runner or deployment identity is compromised.
concepts.label: Development Ecosystem

concepts.decision: Constrain service identities and promotion stages, preserve evidence, and require approval/exception paths appropriate to impact.
concepts.definition: The automated and governed flow that integrates code and promotes artifacts through controlled environments.
concepts.failureExample: A single token that can modify build configuration and deploy removes independent release checks.
concepts.label: Ci Cd

concepts.decision: Use protected branches, attributable review, limited administrative access, and audit of policy/history changes.
concepts.definition: Controlled versioning and review of source and related build/configuration changes.
concepts.failureExample: Changing branch-protection rules just before a merge can bypass review while leaving code history seemingly normal.
concepts.label: Source Control

concepts.decision: Isolate/harden runners and configs, restrict who can invoke or alter them, and preserve attestable build records.
concepts.definition: Protection of build inputs, environment, process, identity, and output from unauthorized modification.
concepts.failureExample: A shared mutable runner image can inject a backdoor into otherwise reviewed releases.
concepts.label: Build Integrity

concepts.decision: Use scoped retrieval, rotation, redaction, audit, and separation per environment/role; respond immediately to leakage.
concepts.definition: Managed lifecycle control for sensitive credentials used by developers, runners, services, and deployments.
concepts.failureExample: A deployment key printed in a CI log can be reused to bypass later pipeline controls.
concepts.label: Secrets Management

concepts.decision: Approve/pin/review dependencies, track transitive components, and test/authorize updates through the release process.
concepts.definition: Governance of component selection, versions, inventories, vulnerabilities, licenses, updates, and owners.
concepts.failureExample: A transitive package takeover can alter builds without a direct developer commit.
concepts.label: Dependency Management

concepts.decision: Identify trust dependencies and define provenance/response controls for code, packages, tools, builders, keys, and artifact stores.
concepts.definition: The broader external and internal chain of software inputs, services, people, and transformations that create a delivered product.
concepts.failureExample: A trusted library can be substituted in transit or by a compromised publisher account.
concepts.label: Supply Chain

misconceptions.claim: A private repository makes source trustworthy.
misconceptions.correction: Repository access, review, identity, dependencies, runners, and release provenance all require controls.

outcome: Select layered controls for a development toolchain and explain how they prevent unauthorized change, leakage, and untrusted artifacts.

sections.body: Use role separation, least privilege, protected branches, code review, signed commits or artifacts where appropriate, reproducible builds, dependency pinning and review, isolated runners, secret management, hardened development environments, artifact repositories, and provenance. Protect CI/CD service identities and distinguish source, build, test, and production privileges.
keyPoints: A compromised build service can undermine otherwise secure source code.
Dependencies and build outputs require inventory and provenance.
Secrets belong in managed stores, not source code or logs.
sections.title: Control people, tools, and artifacts

sections.body: Configuration management, change approval, environment separation, pipeline logging, vulnerability and license review, rollback, patching, and incident response keep the ecosystem trustworthy. Development and operations need shared ownership of emergency changes and evidence. Maturity models help assess process capability but do not replace risk judgment.
keyPoints: Change controls should preserve speed with traceability and rollback.
Pipeline logs are security evidence and may contain sensitive data.
Maturity measures improvement in process capability, not absence of vulnerabilities.
sections.title: Manage change and operations
